svg.title: Remotely triggered black hole: how a single host is sacrificed at the network entry, what it costs, and where it sits relative to scrubbing
svg.desc: Top: the mechanism in four steps. A server is under a volumetric attack; a trigger - flow data, a threshold, or a person - decides to act; the operator advertises the host's /32 with the RTBH community and no-export so the route stays inside the autonomous system; every edge router matches the community and rewrites the next hop to a static route pointing at null0, so the packet is dropped at the first router it reaches and the internal links and the server itself are protected. Middle left: the price - the same address is now unreachable for legitimate users too, which is self-inflicted damage, so the decision needs a named owner and a written definition of "business can be sacrificed briefly". Middle right: when it fits and when it does not - a severe attack on a single address or subnet fits; a wide address range or a business that cannot be interrupted does not. Bottom: the escalation ladder - cloud scrubbing with anycast diversion first, on-premises scrubbing second, per-IP black hole third, per-subnet black hole only as an explicit last resort with a timer. A design with black holing but no scrubbing converts every denial of service problem into "shut the business down".
svg.text: RTBH: make one address disappear from routing so the attack dies at the front door
The traffic is dropped at the first router it reaches, which protects the links and the server - at the cost of the service itself
FOUR STEPS, ALL OF THEM CONFIGURATION YOU CAN PREPARE IN ADVANCE
① Attack on 192.0.2.1
Volumetric, and the uplink is already
saturated before anyone notices
② Trigger
Flow threshold, scrubbing centre,
or a human on an approved runbook
③ Announce the /32
With the RTBH community and
no-export so it stays inside the AS
④ Every edge drops it
Route map matches the community,
next hop is rewritten to a null0 route
ip route 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.255 Null0 plus route-map RTBH-IN: match community RTBH → set ip next-hop 192.0.2.1
The static route is a config artefact, not a policy: it exists only so the rewritten next hop has somewhere to point. Nothing else may use that address.
THE PRICE · THE ADDRESS GOES DARK FOR EVERYONE
Legitimate users are dropped by the same rule as the attacker. There is no
"attack-only" version of this tool - that is what scrubbing is for.
So the design needs three things in writing:
a named owner who may trigger it · a definition of "this service may be
sacrificed briefly" per business system · a timer and a review after it fires
WHEN IT FITS, WHEN IT DOES NOT
Fits: a severe attack on one address or one small subnet
where the business can be offline for minutes to hours
Does not fit: an attack spread over a wide range (you cannot
null-route half the estate), or a service that must not stop
Better: scrubbing centre drops only the attack; cloud scrubbing diverts by anycast
THE ESCALATION LADDER · ALWAYS IN THIS ORDER
1 · Cloud / anycast scrubbing
Attack absorbed upstream; users keep
working. Needs a contract, not a config
2 · On-prem scrubbing
Divert and clean, then reinject.
Needs capacity and a divert design
3 · RTBH per host
Sacrifice one address. Blast radius
known, timer required
4 · RTBH per subnet
Last resort, explicit approval,
and a review even if it worked
Design judgement:
a design with RTBH but no scrubbing turns every denial of service into "shut down the business". RTBH is the safety net, never the plan.
